Tribal town / historical name

Abihka

Also find this entry through: Abihka / Arbeka · Muscogee town history

Abihka names an important part of Muscogee town history, with ancestral connections to Alabama’s Coosa and Choccolocco valleys and continuing Arbeka community life in Oklahoma. Public Muscogee interpretation connects ancestral grounds, forced removal, and the return to those homelands. Historical records use related names at several geographical and political scales, so each source’s date and scope matter.

Read the sources [1] Muscogee (Creek) Nation / City of Oxford; transcription hosted by the Historical Marker Database [2] Mvskoke Media

Names & relationshipsAbihka is part of Muscogee tribal-town history. Arbeka’s public homeland marker explicitly pairs Arbeka and Abihka; historical records also describe Abihkutci, Talladega, and other related or similarly named towns. Those names require date-specific treatment. Natchez connections appear in the historical literature, but do not make all Natchez or Muscogee communities interchangeable or establish a separate modern Abihka national government.
An expanded introduction, with sources reviewed.This profile develops several themes through identified sources. Citations connect each section to its evidence; remaining gaps appear below. It has not been reviewed or endorsed by the community.
01

Begin with Arbeka’s public account

At Choccolocco Park in Oxford, Alabama, a marker headed Muscogee (Creek) Nation identifies its speakers as Arbeka (Abihka). It describes the place as their ancestors’ ceremonial ground, remembers forced removal to Oklahoma, and explains that the people carried their sacred fire west. It connects place names and stories passed between generations with continuing responsibilities to the homeland. This public statement provides a community perspective that older outsiders’ town lists cannot supply. Muscogee Media’s account of the Nation’s 2022 return festival likewise identifies the park with the original Arbeka grounds. These sources establish a living ancestral relationship while leaving the detailed histories of individual towns and families to further research.

Read the sources [1] Muscogee (Creek) Nation / City of Oxford; transcription hosted by the Historical Marker Database [2] Mvskoke Media

02

Abihka, Abihkutchi, and the scope of a name

John R. Swanton’s 1922 study describes Abihka as an old Muscogee division and one of the confederacy’s foundation towns. He also records uncertainty about the name’s derivation and differences among earlier explanations. A single confident English translation would conceal that disagreement. His discussion distinguishes an Abihkutci associated with Abihka from another associated with Okfuskee and warns about similarly named towns. Benjamin Hawkins’s 1798–99 account calls a particular settlement Au-be-coo-che, while reporting that elders sometimes used Au-be-cuh more broadly for the nation. A researcher therefore needs to identify whether a document concerns a settlement, an affiliated grouping, or a wider political name before placing it on a map.

Read the sources [4] Smithsonian Institution, Bureau of American Ethnology [5] Georgia Historical Society / Digital Library of Georgia

03

A landscape of settlements, springs, and family connections

Hawkins places Au-be-coo-che on Nau-che creek, several miles from the Coosa River, and describes scattered settlement on both sides of a fertile creek valley. His account notes limestone springs and wooded slopes and credits the elder Co-tau-lau for information about older customs. It is a federal agent’s dated account, shaped by his own interests in land and agriculture. The 2023 Choccolocco archaeological report adds a different method: comparison of census, land-allotment, and family records. Its discussion links Jim Fife of pre-removal Choccolocco with Arbeka through a 1927 affidavit by his grandson Dorsey Fife. The report presents this as evidence connecting named communities across removal; its archival references remain important leads for independent checking.

Read the sources [5] Georgia Historical Society / Digital Library of Georgia [3] Robert E. Perry & Associates, Inc. / City of Oxford

04

Reading the mounds and the public archaeological record

The Alabama Indigenous Mound Trail describes the Choccolocco complex around Boiling Spring as a landscape with earthen and stone constructions made and changed over a long period. It distinguishes early mound-building phases from the Abihka ceremonial ground documented before removal. Its account connects stone constructions with recorded oral histories of a town lost in water. Those interpretations should retain their stated sources and uncertainties. The much longer 2023 public report explains its research methods and credits Muscogee preservation staff and elders, including Arnold Taylor of Arbeka. It offers substantial evidence alongside hypotheses that require further investigation; every interpretation is not a settled conclusion shared by all community members.

Read the sources [6] Alabama Indigenous Mound Trail / University of Alabama Museums [3] Robert E. Perry & Associates, Inc. / City of Oxford

05

Land loss, removal, and the limits of treaty promises

The 1832 Treaty with the Creeks is essential context for the records of Choccolocco and neighboring towns. Article 1 ceded Creek lands east of the Mississippi. Article 2 provided individual land selections and a census, including arrangements for selections by members of the same town. Article 12 stated that people were free to remain or emigrate. Reading those promises beside the Arbeka marker’s memory of forced removal makes their limits visible. The treaty concerns the Creek Nation broadly; it should not be relabeled a separate Abihka treaty. Its text records negotiated provisions and United States commitments, and does not demonstrate that those commitments were honored.

Read the sources [7] Smithsonian National Museum of the American Indian, Native Knowledge 360° [1] Muscogee (Creek) Nation / City of Oxford; transcription hosted by the Historical Marker Database

06

Oklahoma grounds and changing historical descriptions

Swanton’s Modern Square Grounds of the Creek Indians, published in 1931, identifies an Abihka or Talladega ground near Henryetta. Its introduction dates his renewed field investigation to 1929, while its Abihka discussion also references information from Jim Star and a photograph made in 1912. Swanton revises parts of his earlier account and acknowledges that arrangements could change within a town. This is useful evidence of a named community and the history of documentation. Its title’s word modern belongs to the early twentieth century. The report should not be used as a description of present leadership, a current ceremonial schedule, or permission to reproduce sacred practices.

Read the sources [8] Smithsonian Institution, Smithsonian Miscellaneous Collections 85(8)

07

A Muscogee writer, the Gate Town, and resistance to allotment

In his January 31, 1902 Indian Journal essay, Muscogee writer Charles Gibson connects Arbeka’s historical warning and protective role with the name Gate Town. He identifies Chitto Harjo with Arbeka and uses that association to comment on resistance to United States policy. The Sequoyah Research Center’s edition preserves both Gibson’s writing and modern editorial notes, which readers should distinguish. Kenneth W. McIntosh’s specialist biography of Harjo provides further context: it places his birth at Arbeka and follows his opposition to allotment, political organizing, and testimony. Harjo’s experience illustrates a particular person’s struggle over land and sovereignty. It does not establish that every Arbeka person supported the same strategy.

Read the sources [9] American Native Press Archives and Sequoyah Research Center, University of Arkansas at Little Rock [10] The Encyclopedia of Oklahoma History and Culture, Oklahoma Historical Society

08

An individual family’s path of cultural reconnection

Muscogee Media’s 2022 account follows Sten Joddi’s experience of reconnecting with cultural life. He recalled hearing that family members came from Arbeka but having few opportunities to participate as a child, and then shared a festival dance with his daughters. The article explicitly describes the festival event as a demonstration and includes different views about it. This gives readers an extended individual account of family connections, interrupted learning, and renewed participation. It should not stand in for everyone’s experience or be turned into a description of a private Arbeka ceremony. Public reporting can document a person’s own story while leaving the authority and internal life of the community distinct.

Read the sources [11] Mvskoke Media

09

Returning to the homeland and shaping public history

The inaugural Reyicepes festival in Oxford brought Muscogee citizens, leaders, artists and local residents together in 2022. Mvskoke Media reports ancestral-trail walks, cultural activities and educational partnerships. Separate reporting by Nancy Marie Spears adds original interviews: preservation manager RaeLynn A. Butler identifies the pre-removal Arbeka site and work by city and tribal officials to protect nearby lands. National Council representative Galen Cloud contrasts his journey to Alabama with his ancestors’ forced journey west, emphasizes the importance of present visibility, and describes the continued importance of the fire carried from the homeland. These are specific, attributed interpretations of return and preservation. They do not establish a completed land transfer, title ownership or a single view held by every Arbeka person.

Read the sources [2] Mvskoke Media [12] Gaylord News / Source New Mexico [1] Muscogee (Creek) Nation / City of Oxford; transcription hosted by the Historical Marker Database

What needs further research

  • Seek additional Arbeka-authorized public history and review of preferred names, the town relationships summarized here, and the cultural suitability of archival descriptions.
  • Inspect the original Dorsey Fife affidavit, the relevant land-allotment ledgers and census pages, and the maps behind the 2023 report rather than relying solely on its archival synthesis.
  • Deepen the distinction between historical Abihka, Abihkutci, Abihka-in-the-west, Talladega and Choccolocco communities; similar spellings and reused names do not by themselves establish identical locations or institutions.
  • Expand community-specific evidence on language learning, schooling, livelihoods, women’s experiences, and life beyond the selected public reports. No present speaker, membership, or population total is asserted.
  • Add community-led accounts of Natchez relationships and of removal and allotment experiences; older authors’ assimilation claims and one leader’s biography do not represent every family.
  • Follow the Oxford educational and preservation partnerships with dated evaluations of outcomes, distinguishing plans from completed work.

Twelve inspected resources support a developed historical and community reading profile. The count is separate from research completion or community review. The community marker and 2022 return reporting now substantiate a public Arbeka–Abihka homeland connection that was missing from the earlier guide. Detailed family and institutional histories remain open.
